summary: Pupils aged 9–11 compare Arctic and Antarctic ecosystems systematically rather than listing animals. The organising idea is a structural contrast with a cause: the Arctic is a largely frozen ocean ringed by land joined to other continents, so it has BOTH tundra (land) and marine ecosystems, supporting land mammals (caribou, Arctic foxes, musk oxen), sea-ice hunters such as polar bears, and indigenous human communities; Antarctica is a high continent almost entirely covered by ice, extremely cold, and isolated by the Southern Ocean, so its land is nearly bare of plants and has no land mammals, and life crowds into the surrounding sea. Beneath the difference lies a shared base — phytoplankton feeding krill/zooplankton — on which both short, productive food chains depend. Both regions are disproportionately affected by climate change (they are warming fast and losing sea ice that many animals rely on) and by human activity such as fishing; in this teaching model, the short chains help show why harm to the base spreads upward. Build, sort, and reason activities are proposed to make the compare/contrast active; a dialogue or categorise check are offered as companions.
misconceptions: The two polar ecosystems are basically the same — one has major land ecosystems and people, the other is almost all marine
Antarctica has lots of land animals — its land has almost no plants or land mammals; the life is in the sea
Humans aren't part of polar ecosystems — Arctic indigenous communities are integral to the Arctic system
Polar food chains are long and complex — they are short and intense, built on phytoplankton and krill
Only one pole is threatened — both are disproportionately affected by climate change and human activity

activities.title: Build both poles side by side
steps: On an Arctic panel, stock a tundra with mosses, caribou and foxes, add a human community, AND stock the surrounding sea with seals, fish and whales — notice land and ocean both fill up.

Switch to an Antarctic panel: try to stock the land and find it stays almost empty (a few mosses, no land mammals, no permanent human community) while penguins, seals and whales pile into the surrounding sea.
At the base of both panels, trace a shared conveyor showing phytoplankton feeding krill/zooplankton that feed everything above.
Drag a 'warming' or 'fishing' stressor across both systems and watch each short food chain wobble.
State in one sentence the single structural difference that explains why the Arctic has land AND sea life while Antarctica's life is mostly in the sea.
activities.insight: One structural difference — ocean-ringed-by-land (Arctic) versus an isolated, ice-covered continent ringed by ocean (Antarctic) — shapes who can reach and survive where, yet both ecosystems rest on the same phytoplankton/krill-zooplankton base, and in this model their short food chains show how harm to that base spreads to everything above.

activities.title: Compare-and-contrast table
steps: Fill in a side-by-side table with rows for land life, marine life, humans, producers, and threats for the Arctic and the Antarctic.
For each row, tap the paired ecosystem diagrams (Arctic tundra+sea vs Antarctic sea-dominated) to check what belongs where.
Mark the row that is most clearly the SAME for both poles (producers: phytoplankton, eaten by krill/zooplankton) and write why that shared base matters.
activities.insight: A systematic multi-factor frame (land, sea, humans, producers, threats) reveals both the differences and the common engine beneath them, avoiding a mere animal list.

activities.title: Sort to the correct pole and explain why
steps: Sort cards (polar bear, caribou, penguin, indigenous community, moss, krill, whale, phytoplankton) to Arctic, Antarctic, or both.
For any card placed in only one pole, give the reason — e.g. 'wild penguins live almost entirely in the Southern Hemisphere; polar bears live only in the far north; they never meet in the wild'.

Answer a reasoning probe: 'Reindeer graze on Arctic land but no large animals graze on the Antarctic mainland — why?' and 'If krill numbers crashed, what happens to whales, penguins and seals, and why?'
activities.insight: Correct categorisation plus a stated reason shows the learner links geography to what can live where and recognises the shared, fragile krill base. A sort checks classification but does not by itself elicit the full explanation, so the stated-reason step is needed to reach the reasoning.

activities.title: Talk it through: why are the two poles so different?
steps: Respond to the prompt: 'Polar bears live in the Arctic hunting seals on the sea ice; penguins live in the Antarctic. Why do you never find them living together, and why do big Antarctic animals almost all feed from the SEA rather than the land? Tell me, then tell me WHY the two poles are so different for animals.'
Extend to a transfer case: 'What if a land bridge connected Antarctica to South America — could land animals walk there, and would the ice and cold still stop most of them from living there?'
activities.insight: Verbalising the geographic cause (ocean ringed by land vs continent ringed by ocean → what can reach and live there → sea-based food webs) is intended to consolidate the explanation and to probe transfer.

checkQuestion: Polar bears live in the Arctic, hunting seals out on the sea ice; penguins live in the Antarctic. Why do you never find polar bears and penguins living together, and why do the big Antarctic animals almost all get their food from the SEA rather than the land? Tell me, and then tell me WHY the two poles are so different for animals.
checkAnswer: The Arctic is a frozen OCEAN surrounded by continents, so land animals (polar bears, foxes, reindeer) can reach it and it has land-and-sea food webs; Antarctica is a continent isolated by the vast Southern Ocean, so almost nothing can cross to live on the land — its large animals (penguins, seals, whales) all feed from the sea. Both food webs rest on tiny phytoplankton eaten by krill, so the chains are short, which makes them productive but vulnerable: losing one link (like krill) hits everything above it.
